routes.description: The defender’s route applies the causal principle to a universe whose finite temporal beginning is established by arguments against an actual infinite and against formation by successive addition, then identifies a personal agent as the best explanation of the universe’s first effect.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that the past is finite, that the universe consequently began and has a cause, and that an eternal impersonal mechanism cannot explain a temporally first universe whereas personal agency can.

bridges.description: The Kalam shows that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
A beginningless past would contain an actually infinite number of events; because such an actual infinite cannot exist, the temporal series and universe began.
Hilbert-style concrete scenarios reveal that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible, despite the consistency of infinite set theory.
An actually infinite temporal series cannot be formed by successive addition or completed by counting down from a beginningless past.
An eternal impersonal cause would produce its effect eternally or not at all, while a personal agent can freely originate a temporally first universe.

routes.description: The critic’s route argues that the Kalam does not exclude a beginningless material reality and that its paradoxes and conceptual analysis leave coherent infinite-past and impersonal-cause alternatives available.
routes.successCriteria: Show that actual-infinite scenarios establish strangeness rather than impossibility, that successive-addition reasoning does not rule out a beginningless series ending in the present, or that an impersonal indeterministic cause can explain a first universe without a personal creator.

bridges.description: The Kalam does not show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
The Kalam’s finitude and personhood inferences fail to exclude coherent beginningless-past or impersonal-origin alternatives, so its conclusion is not established.
The unusual behavior of Hilbert’s Hotel does not entail that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible.
The impossibility of reaching the end of an endless count does not establish the impossibility of reaching the present end of a beginningless countdown.
An impersonal indeterministic cause could originate the universe at one time, so a personal cause is not uniquely required.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: If fundamental physics is ontologically decisive, a universe-pervading quantum field may be the sole substance and particles and ordinary objects merely its excitations.
moves.attributionBasis: The span continues Malpass’s response about substances and ends immediately before Craig’s explicit reply concerning physicists and human nature.
moves.selectionRationale: This is a bounded argumentative proposal about fundamental ontology, but it does not itself supply a reason concerning past finitude, actual-infinite impossibility, successive addition, or a personal first cause.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Even if all material objects are excitations of quantum fields, physicists cannot infer that a person is only material, because mind-body dualism allows a nonmaterial soul.
moves.attributionBasis: The event span begins with a marked reply and its defense of mind-body dualism is continuous with Craig’s immediately preceding warning not to trust physicists about human nature.
moves.selectionRationale: The passage contains a single objection to drawing conclusions about persons from physical ontology, but it does not advance the Kalam’s finite-past, causal-origin, or personal-creator inference.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: A beginningless temporal series would instantiate an actually infinite number of past events; because an actual infinite cannot exist in reality, the past is finite and the universe began to exist.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Craig to present his philosophical arguments, and the marked response states Craig’s first finitude argument in one uninterrupted turn.
moves.selectionRationale: The span contains the complete inference from the impossibility of an actual infinite through a finite event series to the universe’s beginning.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Hilbert’s Hotel would behave strangely by accommodating new guests despite every room being occupied, but that strangeness is insufficient to establish that such a hotel could not exist.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Alex by name, and the marked response directly answers whether the scenarios demonstrate impossibility.
moves.selectionRationale: This compact span isolates Malpass’s distinction between unusual infinite behavior and metaphysical impossibility without adding his later independent examples.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: Counting upward and counting down from a beginningless past are asymmetric: one cannot reach the end of an endless sequence, but a beginningless sequence can nevertheless possess a present endpoint.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Malpass’s uninterrupted explanation of his objection to the indirect successive-addition argument, following his explicit division of that argument into types.
moves.selectionRationale: The span states one self-contained asymmetry objection and ends after identifying the chronological gap, before the subsequent exchange about a particular counter.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: If a beginningless countdown could finish today, it could have finished at any earlier past point; then the counter could never be found counting, contradicting the hypothesis that the countdown occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: A brief moderator acknowledgment precedes this span, after which Craig continues the countdown argument in the position-specific first person and Malpass responds only later.
moves.selectionRationale: The passage isolates Craig’s completion-time contradiction as a single reason that a countdown formed throughout a beginningless past is impossible.

moves.speaker: Alex Malpass
moves.proposition: An indeterministic impersonal mechanism could happen to initiate time, and its unexplained timing resembles libertarian free choice closely enough that personal agency is not uniquely required.
moves.attributionBasis: The span continues Malpass’s marked answer to the moderator’s personhood question and ends immediately before Craig’s reply rejecting a scientifically plausible impersonal account.
moves.selectionRationale: The passage develops one coherent alternative to the personal-cause inference and contrasts that alternative directly with agent causation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Because no scientifically plausible impersonal indeterministic account explains why a nonphysical state produced the universe only finitely long ago, the universe’s origin is best explained by a personal agent.
moves.attributionBasis: The span begins with Craig’s marked reply to Malpass’s impersonal-mousetrap proposal and concludes with his explicit endorsement of the traditional personal-agent inference.
moves.selectionRationale: The bounded response connects a finitely timed cosmic origin, causal explanation, and a personal agent, thereby supporting the complete motion-level conclusion.
